text: Coconut octopuses carry coconut shell halves around and put them together as a shelter when they need one. Scientists count this as tool use, which is rare in invertebrates.

text: To carry its shells, a coconut octopus stacks them, tucks them under its body and walks on stiffened arms. Scientists call it stilt-walking.

real: In a Seattle Aquarium study, some giant Pacific octopuses repeatedly jetted water at a floating bottle to push it around, which researchers described as play.
why: Split; 'octopuses really do play' generalized from a small study (two of the octopuses tested), so the real part names the study.

source.publisher: The Common Reader (Washington University in St. Louis)
source.title: Alien Intelligence

searchNote: Search found accounts of the 1999 Seattle Aquarium study in which two octopuses repeatedly jetted floating pill bottles against the current; the counts tested differ between accounts (8 vs 10), so numbers were left out.

text: In the tank, a calm octopus sits still and blends into its surroundings. Wild octopuses can change the color and texture of their skin to hide in plain sight.
game: In the tank, a calm octopus sits still and blends into its surroundings.
real: Wild octopuses can change the color and texture of their skin to hide in plain sight.
why: Split game behavior from the wild fact.

source.title: Cephalopods: Octopus, Squid, Cuttlefish, and Nautilus

searchNote: Smithsonian cephalopod page covers color and texture change for camouflage.

text: In the tank, a shy seahorse keeps to the thickest plants. Wild seahorses rely on camouflage, blending in among seagrass, coral and mangroves.
game: In the tank, a shy seahorse keeps to the thickest plants.
real: Wild seahorses rely on camouflage, blending in among seagrass, coral and mangroves.
why: Split; 'where wild ones are hardest to spot' restated as the sourced camouflage fact.
searchNote: Florida Museum says lined seahorses rely on coloring and texture to camouflage themselves among coral, seagrass or mangroves.

text: In the tank, a calm seahorse stays anchored to one spot for hours. Wild lined seahorses wrap their tails around coral, seaweed or seagrass to stay put, and tend to stay in the same territory their whole lives.
game: In the tank, a calm seahorse stays anchored to one spot for hours.
real: Wild lined seahorses wrap their tails around coral, seaweed or seagrass to stay put, and tend to stay in the same territory their whole lives.
why: Split; 'hold one stem most of the day' replaced with the sourced behavior.
searchNote: Florida Museum says lined seahorses wrap their prehensile tails around coral, seaweed and plants and tend to stay in the same territory their whole lives.

text: In the tank, a curious seahorse turns one eye toward anything new while the other keeps watch. A seahorse can move each eye on its own, looking two ways at once.
game: In the tank, a curious seahorse turns one eye toward anything new while the other keeps watch.
real: A seahorse can move each eye on its own, looking two ways at once.
why: Split game behavior from the wild fact.

source.title: 10 Things You Never Knew About Seahorses

searchNote: Smithsonian says seahorse eyes move independently.

text: In the tank, friendly seahorses link tails and drift together. Wild seahorse pairs link tails during their courtship dances.
game: In the tank, friendly seahorses link tails and drift together.
real: Wild seahorse pairs link tails during their courtship dances.
why: Split; tail-linking is a courtship behavior of pairs, not general friendliness.
searchNote: Shedd describes courting seahorses twining tails and promenading with tails still linked.

text: In the tank, a bold seahorse swims out into open water more often.
game: In the tank, a bold seahorse swims out into open water more often.
why: Split; 'wild ones only do it to find a mate' is an unsupported 'only' claim, so real is null.
searchNote: No source found.

text: Clownfish fathers guard their eggs, fanning water over them and picking out any that go bad.
searchNote: Aquarium of the Pacific says the male fans the eggs to aerate and clean them, eats infertile or damaged ones and chases off predators.

text: A damselfish father guards his eggs, chasing off would-be egg thieves and fanning the eggs to keep fresh water flowing over them.
why: 'Fish far bigger than he is' is not stated in sources; reworded to sourced egg care.
searchNote: Garibaldi (a damselfish) pages describe the male driving away intruders and fanning and grooming the eggs.

text: A watchman goby father guards the eggs and fans them with his fins to keep them supplied with oxygen.
why: 'In a hollow under a rock' does not fit the game's watchman goby, which lives in a burrow with a shrimp.
searchNote: Search summary attributed to an aquarium resource on watchman gobies that the male guards the eggs and fans them for oxygen (verify on the Aquarium of the Pacific page).

text: A royal gramma father builds a nest in a small hole in the reef and guards and cleans the eggs laid there.
why: No source found for lining the nest with seaweed; kept the sourced parts.
searchNote: UWI sheet says males build nests in small openings in the substrate and protect, maintain and clean the den with the eggs.

why: Same claim as p59, with the same over-certain 'eat nothing'.

text: Angelfish pairs rise up off the reef together to spawn, and their eggs drift away on the current.
why: 'At dusk' is not consistent across species (some spawn at dusk, some early morning); dropped.
searchNote: Florida Museum angelfish profiles describe pairs rising in the water column to release eggs and sperm; eggs are pelagic.

text: Mandarin pairs rise together at dusk and release their eggs to drift.
searchNote: Aquarium of the Pacific says mandarins spawn after sunset, a female and male rising together; the eggs are pelagic (verify 'rise' wording).

text: An octopus mother guards her eggs in her den: she keeps them clean, sends fresh water over them, and rarely leaves until they hatch.
why: 'Hangs her eggs in strings from the roof of her den' describes species like the giant Pacific octopus; the game's coconut octopus lays its eggs inside a shell. Made general.
searchNote: Aquarium of the Pacific GPO page says the mother keeps eggs clean, fans or squirts water over them and does not eat while brooding.
